title: Julia Kristeva
keyWorks: Powers of Horror: An Essay on Abjection (1980)
The Sense and Non-Sense of Revolt (1996)
Female Genius — a trilogy on Hannah Arendt, Melanie Klein and Colette (1999–2002)
summary: Julia Kristeva is a philosopher, linguist, psychoanalyst and novelist who came to Paris from Bulgaria in 1965 and became one of the central figures of poststructuralism. She coined the term “intertextuality,” showed how bodily rhythm and the strict order of meaning meet in language, and wrote books on abjection, love, melancholia and the stranger who lives in each of us. Kristeva teaches us to see in the darkest and most “awkward” feelings not a breakdown but the work of the boundaries from which our “I” is made.
onEmotions: Kristeva distinguishes two layers in the psyche. The “semiotic” is ancient and bodily: rhythm, pulse, intonation, drives that live in us before words. The “symbolic” is language, rules, names, meaning. A feeling is born where the two meet, and much suffering, for Kristeva, is experience that has not yet found its signs. Her main path is not to suppress a feeling but to translate it into form: a word, a story, an image, music. For her a person is a “subject in process,” never finished. Even disgust, which she called “abjection,” and black melancholia are described without judgment — as ways in which a fragile “I” builds and guards its boundaries.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is exhausting, and it is not a sign that something is wrong with you. Kristeva distinguished two layers in our psyche. The “symbolic” is words, grammar, plans, the names of things. The “semiotic” is an older layer: rhythm, tension, pulse, intonation, everything that lives in the body before words. Anxiety, from her point of view, is like a semiotic wave that hasn’t yet found its words: your heart pounds, something inside goes round in circles, and you can’t name it. Kristeva spoke of the human being as a “subject in process”: we are never finished, and tension is part of that movement. As a psychoanalyst, she cared about something else too: an experience becomes easier to bear when it is gradually translated into signs — into words, images, a story. Not to cancel it, but to give it a place.
anxiety.practice: First describe your anxiety as if it were music: what is its tempo, its volume, its rhythm? Then try to find one or two words for it.

fear.text: Fear is an ancient and honest feeling; it protects what you hold dear. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva examines Freud’s famous case of Little Hans — a boy who was afraid of horses. She shows that the object of a phobia can be like a condensation: many vague fears that have no name of their own gather into one clear image. The horse frightened him not only as a horse — it carried a whole tangle of anxieties. From Kristeva’s perspective, adult fears are sometimes built the same way: a concrete occasion — a conversation, a doctor, a journey — takes on the weight of something much wider. That doesn’t make the fear imaginary. But if you gently ask what else is sounding in it, it often becomes more understandable and a little less all-powerful.
fear.practice: Finish the sentence: “I’m afraid of this, and maybe I’m also afraid of…” Don’t look for the right answer — just see what comes.

sadness.text: You don’t need to be ashamed of sadness, or hurry it on its way. In Black Sun, Kristeva offers an unexpected view: sorrow is not only pain but also a kind of support. When something inside falls apart, sadness gathers a person into one whole feeling: heavy, perhaps, but whole. It seems to say, “There was a loss here, and it matters.” Kristeva saw the way forward not in suppressing sadness but in giving it form — in words, music, drawing, conversation. It’s no accident that her book is full of readings of artists and writers — Holbein, Dostoevsky, Nerval, Duras — who turned sorrow into signs. When sadness takes on a form, it stops being mute and becomes part of your story.
sadness.practice: If your sadness were a color, a sound or a kind of weather — what would it be? Write it down in a word or two.

grief.text: Grief is love that has nowhere left to go, and it keeps no proper timetable. In Black Sun, Kristeva describes how language itself is born. A child can say “mama” because mama is sometimes not there: the word appears where we come to accept absence. Kristeva puts it almost as a paradox: I have lost what is most precious, but because I have agreed to lose it, I can find it again in signs. For someone grieving this is not a substitute consolation: signs do not bring a person back. But they let you keep your bond with them — in stories, words, names, rituals. From Kristeva’s point of view, grief that finds its speech does not become less than love; it becomes love’s continuation.
grief.practice: Write down one very concrete detail about the person you’ve lost: a gesture, a favorite little word, a scent. Let it be kept in words.

loneliness.text: Loneliness can be very sharp, and it doesn’t prove that no one needs you. Kristeva, who came to Paris from Bulgaria as a young scholar, writes in Strangers to Ourselves about the particular experience of the foreigner: living between languages, feeling that you are never quite heard. But the book’s central idea — following Freud and his notion of the “uncanny,” something at once familiar and strange — is that the strange lives inside each of us. We don’t coincide even with ourselves. From Kristeva’s perspective, loneliness is not your personal flaw but a heightened version of the common human condition: we are all a little foreign. Paradoxically, this shared condition can become a bridge: someone else may be lonely in just the same way.
loneliness.practice: Think of one person who, you suspect, is sometimes lonely too. Consider what short message you could send them.

anger.text: Anger is a powerful energy, and it has a right to exist. Kristeva did not divide the drives into “good” and “bad.” In Revolution in Poetic Language she writes about “negativity” — the destructive, rejecting force of the drives, without which there is neither growth nor creativity: for something new to appear, something old must be thrown off. Poets like Lautréamont and Mallarmé, as she saw it, let precisely this force into language and broke the usual order of sentences. It doesn’t follow that anger should be poured out on people. What follows is something else: anger has a form in which it can be lived through without harm — rhythm, movement, a sharp word on paper. Anger that has found its form often tells you which boundary you want to protect.
anger.practice: For a couple of minutes, write down everything that makes you angry, fast, with no punctuation and no addressee. Then reread it and underline which boundary was crossed.

shame.text: Shame makes you want to vanish from other people’s eyes, and it is one of the most tormenting feelings there is. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva draws on the French word propre, which means “clean,” “proper” and “one’s own” all at once. From childhood our “I” is built as something “clean and proper”: we learn to draw boundaries — what in me is acceptable, what must be hidden. From Kristeva’s perspective, shame flares up when that boundary seems to have been breached: something out of place has broken out, and it has been seen. But her analysis shows something else as well: these boundaries are largely set by culture, and the “improper” exists in every human being. Shame speaks of a boundary, not of your worth.
shame.practice: Ask yourself: what boundary of the “proper” do I feel I have crossed? Who drew it for me, and when?

guilt.text: Guilt can be a heavy burden, and the fact that you feel it already speaks of your conscience. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva traces how culture has dealt with what it considered “impure.” In the biblical prescriptions, defilement is external: it is set apart by rules and prohibitions. In Christianity, by her analysis, it moves inward and becomes sin — and with that comes the possibility of putting it into words: repentance, confession, forgiveness through speech. Later, in Black Sun, Kristeva writes of forgiveness not as forgetting the deed but as the gift of a new meaning: what was done is not erased, but it can be given a different continuation. Without drawing religious conclusions, you can take the essential point: guilt is eased not by silent self-punishment but by words.
guilt.practice: Describe in two or three sentences what happened, and then in one sentence what you could do now so that what comes next is different.

envy.text: Envy is an unpleasant but deeply human feeling; everyone who admits it feels it, and so does everyone who doesn’t. Kristeva wrote a major book on the psychoanalyst Melanie Klein, whose late essay is called Envy and Gratitude. Following Klein, she sees envy as one of the earliest feelings: a wish not so much to get someone else’s good thing as to spoil it, because it isn’t mine. Klein and Kristeva speak of this without moralizing. What matters is that envy has a counterweight — gratitude, the capacity to take in what is good and rejoice in it. The two feelings don’t exclude each other: when we notice envy without condemning ourselves, we often make room both for gratitude and for understanding what we are actually missing.
envy.practice: Finish the sentence: “I envy this because I myself would like…” Then name one good thing you already have.

emptiness.text: Emptiness can be worse than pain: no desires, no meaning, words feel like cardboard. In Black Sun, Kristeva wrote about this state with great respect. She spoke of the “Thing” — a loss older than any concrete loss, which cannot be named because it happened before we learned to speak. When this ancient emptiness rises, signs lose their weight: a person speaks, but the words stop meaning anything. Kristeva described it as a broken link between words and feeling. What helps then? From her point of view, the way back begins with the semiotic — with what comes before words: rhythm, melody, color, the voice of someone close. You don’t have to find the meaning of life right away. It’s enough for something small to start sounding again.
emptiness.practice: Listen to one melody, or simply to the sound of rain, footsteps, wind. Don’t judge it — notice whether anything responds in you, even slightly.

confusion.text: Confusion — when your old picture of the world has stopped working and there is no new one yet — is frightening, but there is nothing shameful in it. For Kristeva, a human being is a “subject in process.” The French phrase carries a double meaning: en procès means both “in process” and “on trial,” that is, in question. Our “I” is not a finished statue but constant movement between a stable order of words and meanings and the living forces that wear that order away. In Revolution in Poetic Language, Kristeva shows that it is precisely in moments of disruption, when familiar language can no longer cope, that something new is born. From Kristeva’s perspective, confusion is not a breakdown but a transition: the old form no longer holds, and the new one is still coming together.
confusion.practice: Write down three things you are unsure of right now, and one thing you are at least a little sure of. Let that be enough for today.

fatigue.text: Fatigue is not laziness or a weakness of character, but a signal from the body worth listening to. Kristeva reminds us that we have not only a “symbolic” life — roles, duties, the right words — but also a “semiotic” one: the rhythm of breathing, the pulse, the need for quiet and repetition. Living only in the symbolic is exhausting: you constantly have to measure up, explain, keep up appearances. From Kristeva’s perspective, deep fatigue is the voice of the semiotic layer, long left without attention and now demanding its own rhythm. It asks not for new meanings and tasks but for simple repeated things: rocking, warm water, quiet music. Rest, in this logic, is not a reward for work done but a return to your own rhythm.
fatigue.practice: For a minute, find a simple repeating rhythm — breathing, rocking, quiet humming — and allow yourself not to explain anything.

boredom.text: Boredom can be sluggish and dreary, and it too is saying something. In New Maladies of the Soul, Kristeva writes about the modern person surrounded on all sides by ready-made images and standard answers. There is neither time nor room to build an inner life of one’s own — what she called “psychic space.” From Kristeva’s perspective, boredom is the sensation of a language the rhythm has drained out of: everything has been said in advance, everything is the same, nothing pulses. Her remedy is not new entertainment but a return to the living word. It’s no accident she valued poetry so highly: in it, sound, repetition and surprise are joined to meaning again. Boredom can become an invitation to listen for what in you has not yet been said.
boredom.practice: Read a short poem or a favorite song aloud, slowly, listening to the sound. Notice one place where the rhythm caught you.

joy.text: Joy is a beautiful state, and it needs no justification. Kristeva was one of the first to introduce French readers to Mikhail Bakhtin and his idea of carnival — a festival where laughter suspends hierarchies and familiar roles. In her own theory, joy, laughter and music are moments when the semiotic — bodily, rhythmic — breaks freely into the ordered world of words and rules. She has a word for such moments: jouissance — enjoyment, fullness, when the boundary between “I” and the world becomes permeable for an instant. Kristeva did not consider this frivolous: without such flashes the symbolic order would turn to stone. Joy, from this point of view, is not a distraction from life but its renewal.
joy.practice: Notice where joy lives in you right now: in laughter, in movement, in your voice? Let it sound a little — smile, sing a line, take a walk.

love.text: Love is one of the strongest experiences there is, and it has every right to turn a life upside down. In Tales of Love, Kristeva traces love from Narcissus and Plato to the troubadours, Romeo and Juliet, and psychoanalysis. Her central idea: falling in love is a crisis and a renewal of the “I.” In love our boundaries open, our former identity wavers, and we rebuild ourselves around an ideal. Kristeva compared the psyche to an “open system” — a living organism that renews itself only in exchange with another. She does not debunk love as an illusion, although she sees narcissism and idealization in it too. On the contrary, she considers this capacity to shed one’s skin beside another person one of the foundations of a living psyche.
love.practice: Think about it: who have you become — or are you becoming — beside this person? Write down one quality that has emerged in you.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm, gathering feeling, and you want it to last. In her book on Melanie Klein, Kristeva examines Klein’s thinking about gratitude in detail. For Klein it is not politeness but a deep capacity: to receive something good from another, let it inside, and allow it to become part of yourself. Gratitude, for Klein, is the counterweight to envy: where envy spoils the good because it belongs to someone else, gratitude lets it simply be. Kristeva valued this idea because it shows that good things don’t only happen to us — we learn to receive them. From this point of view, your gratitude is no small thing: it is a sign that there is a place inside you where good can come in and stay.
gratitude.practice: Choose one good thing you are grateful for and describe exactly what you received from it — as if you were placing it on a shelf inside yourself.

hope.text: Hope is fragile, and holding on to it is not naive. In This Incredible Need to Believe, Kristeva, who called herself a non-believer, argues that the need to believe is universal and older than any religion. It is born in early childhood, when an infant trusts that it will be heard, that its cry will be answered, that it is being held. Kristeva calls this stage trust in a loving other, present in the child’s world before any rules. From this point of view, hope is not a calculation of odds but a continuation of that first trust: faith that the world is capable of answering. You can protect it even when the evidence is thin. It rests not on a forecast but on the experience that once, you were already held.
hope.practice: Remember a time when help or an answer came even though you had stopped expecting it. Stay with that memory for a minute.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a sweet, aching longing for the past, and there is much tenderness in it. In Time and Sense, Kristeva wrote about Proust — the author in whom the taste of a madeleine dipped in tea suddenly gives the narrator back a whole childhood. She was interested in how a sensation — a taste, a smell, a sound — keeps time better than conscious memory does. This is close to her idea of the semiotic: we have a layer of experience recorded not in words but in rhythms, shades, bodily imprints. From Kristeva’s perspective, nostalgia often longs not so much for events as for this fabric of sensations. And that is why the past is not entirely lost: it lives in the body and answers when it meets a familiar smell or melody.
nostalgia.practice: Recall one sensation from that time — a smell, a sound, a taste, a texture — and describe it in as much detail as you can.

craving.text: A craving is a sharp “I want it now,” and it can feel almost irresistible. This is not a weakness of character. In Black Sun, Kristeva speaks of the “Thing” — an ancient, nameless lack older than any particular desire. Later, in New Maladies of the Soul, she writes about how the modern person tries to plug this lack with quick fixes — shopping, images, substances — so as not to meet it face to face. From Kristeva’s perspective, a craving promises to restore a lost fullness instantly. But a substance or an object cannot be what it seems: it only screens the emptiness for a while. What helps is not fighting yourself, but trying to understand what exactly the craving promises, and looking for another, gentler way to express it.
craving.practice: Ask yourself: “What feeling am I hoping to get right now — calm, warmth, oblivion?” Name it, and notice how the wave of craving rises and gradually subsides.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure, and shame only adds to the weight. As a psychoanalyst, Kristeva looked at it without judgment. In New Maladies of the Soul, she describes a person whose “psychic space” has shrunk — the inner place where pain, desire and loss can become a thought, an image, a word. When there is little of that space, suffering seeks an immediate outlet, and a substance or a habit begins to do the work that speech and close relationships would otherwise do. The path her thinking suggests is to gradually restore that space: to learn to name what hurts, and to share it with those who are able to listen. It is long work, and it doesn’t require you to be perfect.
addiction.practice: Write down in one sentence what feeling the addiction helped you hide from. If you’d like, you can talk about it with people who know this path from the inside — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after — a heavy body, anxiety, embarrassment about last night — calls for gentleness, not a verdict. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva describes “abjection” — an ancient movement of rejection, when we push away from ourselves whatever threatens our boundaries: the nauseating, the unclean, the “not right.” From Kristeva’s perspective, a hangover is often experienced exactly like this: as if your own body and last night had become “not mine,” and you want to distance yourself from them. The revulsion is understandable, but it speaks of breached boundaries, not of you being a bad person. Kristeva believed the abject can be dealt with not only by casting it off but also through words. To gently name what happened is to take your body back.
hangover.practice: Name one thing your body needs right now — water, food, sleep, fresh air — and give it that, as you would for someone you love.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria — a surge when everything seems possible — can be beautiful, and you don’t need to be suspicious of it straight away. Kristeva has a word for such moments: jouissance, an overflowing enjoyment in which the boundary between “I” and the world becomes permeable. She described it as a breakthrough of the semiotic — rhythm, energy, bodiliness — through the usual order. This is not frivolity: without such breakthroughs there would be neither music nor poetry. But Kristeva always showed that the semiotic lives in a pair with the symbolic — word, form, coherence. So a good way to live a high more fully is to give it form: say it, write it, sing it. Then the joy won’t just rush through you — it will stay with you.
euphoria.practice: Write down three words that best capture this state. Let your high have its own small text.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a substance — can feel like a fall, and in it you can easily come to believe that everything good was a lie. That’s an understandable reaction, not the truth about you. From Kristeva’s perspective, the psyche lives in constant oscillation: now a semiotic wave — energy, rhythm, rapture — dissolves boundaries, now the symbolic gathers them again — with rules, tasks, the heaviness of words. The crash is the return of boundaries after they have opened, and it can be painful, like light after darkness. But in the “subject in process” Kristeva saw movement, not a final state. Neither the rise nor the fall is the last chapter. The joy that was there remains real.
crash.practice: Tell yourself: “This is the comedown after a high, not the final word.” Do something very simple and physical — a warm drink, a short walk, a blanket to wrap yourself in.

panic.text: A panic attack is one of the most frightening experiences there is: a wave of terror washes over you, and your body seems to stop obeying. It really is very frightening. Kristeva described how, in moments of intense terror, the familiar order of words and meanings — the symbolic — seems to retreat, leaving the bare semiotic: pulse, breath, trembling. From Kristeva’s perspective, in panic the body speaks its ancient language of rhythm. That is why what helps is not arguing with the terror but a gentle return to simple supports: a slow rhythm of breathing and the most ordinary words — the names of things around you. Such a wave usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. There is nothing you need to decide right now — just breathe and wait for it to pass.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and take a few breaths with a long, slow exhale. Name aloud five objects around you and their colors.

dread.text: Existential dread — the feeling of an abyss, of “what is all this for” — comes to thoughtful people, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva describes the place “where meaning collapses”: encounters with what threatens the very boundary of our existence. But her book is not about surrendering to horror. She shows how people in every age have answered it: with ritual, with religion and above all with art. Literature, from Dostoevsky to Proust and Joyce, in her view, knows how to look at horror and give it form — and in that there is purification, catharsis. From her point of view, meaning is not given to us once and for all, but we create it again and again — through speech, creativity, bonds with others. That work is itself the answer to the abyss.
dread.practice: Write one sentence beginning with “What frightens me is…” and one beginning with “And yet today I hold dear…”.

fomo.text: The fear of missing out — the feeling that real life is happening somewhere without you — is familiar to a great many people. In New Maladies of the Soul, Kristeva writes about a person besieged by a stream of images. The screen offers ready-made pictures of other people’s lives, and less and less room is left for one’s own inner life — for dreams, doubts, unhurried reflection. She called this inner place “psychic space.” From Kristeva’s perspective, the fear of missing out appears when other people’s images begin to replace your own experiences: we compare our complicated lives with someone else’s curated frames. The remedy here is not to fit more in, but to reclaim your right to your own inner time, which nobody photographs.
fomo.practice: Put the screen down and write about one small moment from today that you lived for yourself — no photo, no witnesses.

sleepless.text: A sleepless night drags on, and thoughts in the dark seem heavier than they do by day. This is not your fault. From Kristeva’s perspective, at night the symbolic weakens — the daytime order of plans, tasks and proper words — and the semiotic rises to the surface: scraps of images, rhythms of anxiety, vague sensations of the body. That’s why night thoughts are so hard to reach with logic: arguing with them by reasoning is useless. Kristeva reminded us that our first supports were rhythmic — a voice, rocking, a lullaby. The psyche still responds to this ancient language. Instead of solving daytime problems at night, you can give yourself a simple rhythm. Conclusions reached at night are not necessarily true: in the morning, much looks different.
sleepless.practice: Breathe slowly, silently repeating one soft word on each exhale — “quiet” or “it’s okay.” If an anxious thought comes, tell it: “In the morning.”

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds especially deeply, because the blow comes from where you felt safe. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva notes something striking: abjection — a deep, almost bodily revulsion — is provoked not only by filth but also by the traitor, the liar, the criminal with a clear conscience. Because they reveal the fragility of what we relied on: law, agreement, trust. From Kristeva’s perspective, you can understand why betrayal is felt not simply as sadness but as nausea, as if the ground had gone out from under you. Your reaction is proportionate: the boundary your sense of safety rested on has been destroyed. But this speaks of the other person’s act, not of your naivety. Trusting is not a mistake; it is the foundation of living with people.
betrayal.practice: Write down what exactly you relied on in this relationship. This will help you see what was destroyed — and what of it remains yours.

jealousy.text: Jealousy can burn very fiercely, and it doesn’t make you a bad person. In Tales of Love, Kristeva shows that in love we build our “I” around the other: their gaze and attachment become a mirror in which we see ourselves as loved and significant. She isn’t embarrassed by the word “narcissism”: for her it is a necessary foundation of any love. From Kristeva’s perspective, jealousy is the fear that the mirror will turn toward someone else, and your image of yourself will shatter along with it. Hence its sharpness: what is under threat is not only the relationship but who you feel yourself to be. It helps to reclaim at least part of your footing — what is valuable in you regardless of anyone else’s gaze.
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence: “When I’m jealous, I’m afraid of losing not only him or her, but also myself as…” See which word comes.

resentment.text: Resentment that won’t go away is a heavy load, and it’s understandable that you carry it: you were treated unfairly. In The Sense and Non-Sense of Revolt, Kristeva speaks of “revolt” in the old sense of the word: as a return, a re-examination, a question we put to the past. For her such revolt is a condition of a living psyche: without it a person freezes. From Kristeva’s perspective, two paths can be distinguished. Resentment goes round in circles, repeating the same thing. Revolt returns to the wound in order to question it and find a new meaning. This doesn’t require forgiving what cannot be forgiven. But moving from repetition to questioning can gradually loosen resentment’s grip and give you back your movement.
resentment.practice: Instead of the familiar resentful thought, write down a question to it: “What is this resentment trying to protect in me?”

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts almost physically, and that is no exaggeration. In Tales of Love, Kristeva describes love as a state in which the “I” opens up and rebuilds itself around another. So a breakup is not only the loss of a person: the version of yourself you built together with them collapses too. And in Black Sun she shows that each new loss can awaken older, earliest losses — hence the feeling that it hurts more than it should. From Kristeva’s perspective, this is not weakness but how the psyche is made. But there is hope here too: the capacity for love that opened you to another doesn’t disappear. If you were once able to rebuild yourself beside someone, that capacity remains yours.
heartbreak.practice: Write down one thing you learned about yourself in this love. It stays with you, even if the person is no longer beside you.

impostor.text: The feeling “I’m an impostor and I’m about to be found out” is familiar to many intelligent, experienced people. Kristeva coined a concept that can be unexpectedly comforting here — “intertextuality.” Following Bakhtin, she showed that every text is woven from other texts: it absorbs other people’s words and makes them its own. From Kristeva’s perspective, a person is built the same way. Your skills, manners and thoughts were gathered from teachers, books, colleagues — and this is not forgery but the ordinary way meaning exists. The impostor thinks that somewhere there are “real” people, made out of nothing. But there are none. The difference is not whether what you have is borrowed, but how you have combined and reworked what came from others.
impostor.practice: Name three people or three books you have learned something from. Then write down what you added to it of your own.

quote.text: Any text is constructed as a mosaic of quotations; any text is the absorption and transformation of another.
quote.author: Julia Kristeva

self_hatred.text: When an inner voice keeps insisting that you are disgusting and good for nothing, it hurts terribly — and that voice is not telling the truth about you. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva describes “abjection” — an ancient movement of rejection through which every person, in childhood, learns to separate “I” from “not-I.” She notes that this movement can also turn against oneself: a person begins to push away parts of themselves. For Kristeva this is a mechanism common to all people, not a verdict. The voice of hatred is an echo of a very early way of building boundaries, not a considered assessment of your life. You can notice it as a phenomenon and not agree with it. And the psyche, for Kristeva, is always in process — it can be built differently.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence your inner critic is saying right now, and next to it, how a kind person who knows you would answer it.

helplessness.text: Helplessness — the feeling that nothing depends on you — is one of the hardest feelings, and you don’t have to be ashamed of it. Kristeva, following Freud, reminds us that human life begins in complete helplessness. An infant cannot survive without someone to hold it. So vulnerability is not a defect but our shared foundation. Kristeva also wrote a great deal about this in connection with disability — including in an open letter to the President of France about people with disabilities (2003). Her idea: vulnerability makes us human and connects us to one another. From her point of view, you can see in helplessness not only a dead end but also a reminder that we are not meant to cope alone.
helplessness.practice: Name one very small thing that is within your power right now, and one person to whom you could say, “I’m having a hard time.”

procrastination.text: “I can’t get started” is a state easily mistaken for laziness, though most often that’s not what it is. Kristeva helps us see a conflict between two layers in it. The task lives in the symbolic: deadlines, requirements, the right form, evaluation. But the wish to do something is born in the semiotic — in interest, rhythm, a bodily “I want to.” When the symbolic presses too hard, demanding that you do it right and well from the start, the living impulse freezes. Studying poets like Mallarmé, Kristeva showed that the new is born where rhythm and sound at first run ahead of meaning. From Kristeva’s perspective, it helps to begin not with what’s correct but with what’s alive: a draft, a sketch, a clumsy first sentence that still has movement in it.
procrastination.practice: Give yourself five minutes for a deliberately bad draft: write or do it any old way, as long as there’s rhythm. You can fix it later.

uprooted.text: Being torn from the places you come from is a deep loss, and Kristeva knew it from the inside: at twenty-four she moved from Bulgaria to France and began writing in a foreign language. In Strangers to Ourselves, she describes the foreigner’s experience with great precision: life between two languages, the silence when your native words are of no use to anyone here and the new ones have not yet become your own. She doesn’t prettify this pain. But her key move is to turn the view around: the foreign is not only outside, it lives inside every person, even one who has never left home. Your rootlessness is not a deviation from the norm but a heightened experience of something everyone shares. And in that clarity freedom can appear: you are building yourself, not only inheriting.
uprooted.practice: Write down one word from your native language or home place that is hard to translate. Think about what it holds for you.

quote.text: Strangely, the foreigner lives within us: he is the hidden face of our identity.
quote.author: Julia Kristeva

overload.text: Overload — when there is more information, more messages, more images than your head can hold — is a real burden, not your weakness. In New Maladies of the Soul, Kristeva describes the modern person being filled with images without being given time to process them. She speaks of the shrinking of “psychic space” — the inner place where impressions turn into one’s own thoughts and feelings. When the stream is too dense, impressions are not absorbed but simply pile up as noise. From Kristeva’s point of view, the way out is not to consume faster, but to reclaim the pause. One impression truly lived through and named gives more than a hundred scrolled past.
overload.practice: Pick one impression from today and tell yourself about it in three sentences. The rest you can let go of for now.

unreality.text: The feeling that the world, or you yourself, are somehow not quite real can be strange and unsettling, and it deserves gentle care. In Black Sun, Kristeva describes a state in which words and things seem to lose their weight: everything is visible and understood, but nothing touches you, as if there were glass between you and the world. She explains this as a break in the link between signs and feelings. From Kristeva’s point of view, the way back runs through the semiotic — through the layer of experience older than words: texture, temperature, sound, rhythm. It was simple sensations that first connected us to the world in childhood, and they can still restore a sense of presence. You don’t need to prove to yourself that everything is real — it’s enough to touch.
unreality.practice: Touch three different surfaces near you — something warm, something cool, something rough — and say aloud what your fingers feel.

awe.text: Awe — before mountains, a starry sky, great music — is one of the most powerful experiences, and you want to keep hold of it. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva observes that the abject borders on the sublime: both go beyond the limits of our “I,” but where the abject threatens, the sublime expands us. From Kristeva’s perspective, in awe the “I” for a moment stops being the center, and this is not frightening but freeing: we find ourselves part of something larger than we know how to name. Words fall short — and that is as it should be: here the semiotic is speaking, the rhythm and breath of the world. Such moments don’t need explaining. You can simply allow them, and later remember them tenderly.
awe.practice: Spend a minute in silence with whatever stirred your awe. Then find one word — not an explanation, but a response.

relief.text: Relief is the exhale after long tension, and it deserves to be fully felt. Kristeva has a concept that describes this moment well — catharsis, purification. In Powers of Horror, she shows how ritual and art helped people meet what threatened them, give it form — and come out renewed. Tension doesn’t vanish without a trace: it passes through us, and we end up on the other side. From Kristeva’s perspective, relief is the moment when boundaries that were under threat hold again, and the psyche can relax. Don’t rush straight on to the next task. Let your body notice that the danger has passed.
relief.practice: Take a few slow exhales and notice where in your body the tension has gone: your shoulders, your jaw, your belly? Stay with that sensation.

calm.text: Calm is a state worth cherishing without asking more of it. Kristeva has an image borrowed from Plato — the chora. That is what she called the earliest space of our psyche: not yet words or thoughts, but rhythm, warmth, a voice, rocking, in which an infant feels held. From Kristeva’s perspective, deep calm is a meeting with this ancient layer: when nothing needs to be named or proven, and steady breathing and a quiet rhythm are enough. Such calm is not empty. It nourishes: words and deeds later grow out of it. You can simply be in it, without turning it into a task.
calm.practice: Notice the rhythm around you right now: your breathing, a clock ticking, the noise outside the window. Stay with it for a minute.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful surge, and you want to catch it. Kristeva explains what happens in it in her major theoretical book, Revolution in Poetic Language. There she shows how, in poets like Mallarmé and Lautréamont, the semiotic — rhythm, sound, bodily energy — bursts into the symbolic, into correct language, and remakes it from within. That is how the new is born: not from rules alone and not from pure chaos, but from their meeting. From Kristeva’s perspective, inspiration is the moment when living energy finds its way into form. Let it flow without demanding perfection straight away. You can tidy up the form later, but the flow is worth not letting slip.
inspiration.practice: Write down everything that comes, right now, without correcting. Then mark the one line that has the most life in it.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — secret pleasure at someone else’s failure — is a feeling people rarely admit to, yet almost everyone knows it. It says nothing final about you. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva shows that our “I” holds itself together on the boundary between “me” and “not me.” When someone falls, especially someone who seemed more successful or who hurt us, that boundary is strengthened for a moment: “it happened to them, not to me.” From Kristeva’s perspective, schadenfreude is a brief relief from our own vulnerability, which we glimpsed in another. If you notice this without condemning yourself, the feeling becomes a clue: where do you yourself feel fragile or undervalued? What matters is not the feeling itself but what you do with it.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: “What in me settled down when they stumbled?” Write down the answer without judging it.

contempt.text: Contempt can feel cold and reliable, like armor, and feeling it is human. In Strangers to Ourselves, Kristeva, following Freud, observes that what we push away with dislike in another often turns out to be our own unacknowledged strangeness. We wall ourselves off from “them” so as not to face what troubles us inside. Her conclusion: if we recognize the stranger in ourselves, we won’t have to hate it in others. From Kristeva’s perspective, contempt guards a boundary — between “me, the decent one” and “them.” This doesn’t mean your judgment of another’s actions is wrong. But it’s worth asking what exactly the boundary is protecting — and then the armor may become a little less necessary.
contempt.practice: Name a trait that fills you with contempt, and honestly ask: “When was I myself afraid of turning out like that?”

disgust.text: Disgust — at a situation, at people, even at yourself — is a strong bodily feeling, and there is nothing shameful in it. It is the central theme of Kristeva’s Powers of Horror: An Essay on Abjection. She calls it “abjection” and begins with a simple example: the skin on the surface of milk that makes a child shudder. Abjection, for Kristeva, is the most ancient way we separate “I” from “not-I”: we push away what mixes with us and blurs our boundaries. That is why disgust is provoked not simply by dirt but by the ambiguous, the in-between, what is out of place. This knowledge is freeing: your disgust is not a moral verdict but a signal about a boundary. And what to do with it is up to you.
disgust.practice: Ask yourself: “Which of my boundaries does this violate — bodily, moral, the boundary of my ‘I’?” A word or two in reply is enough.

quote.text: It is thus not lack of cleanliness or health that causes abjection but what disturbs identity, system, order. What does not respect borders, positions, rules. The in-between, the ambiguous, the composite.
quote.author: Julia Kristeva
quote.source: Powers of Horror: An Essay on Abjection (1980)

revenge.text: The wish for revenge can burn, especially when the hurt is deep and unjust. The wish itself is not a crime but a sign of great pain. Kristeva wrote a great deal about how the symbolic — law, speech, recognition — arises in culture as a way of translating destructive drives into something we can live with together. Revenge, from this point of view, often wants not so much to cause pain as to win recognition: for the wrong to be named as wrong, and for you to be seen as the one who was hurt. From Kristeva’s perspective, that recognition is better sought in words than in an act that would extend the chain of destruction. Your wish for justice is legitimate, and there are safer paths for it.
revenge.practice: Write a letter you will never send: what you would want this person to understand. Then keep it or tear it up.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those closest to us — a partner, parents, children — happens to almost everyone, and the shame that follows is just as familiar. Drawing on Melanie Klein, Kristeva shows that love and aggression have been intertwined in our most important relationships since childhood: the person closest to us both demands the most of us and can hurt us the most. She stresses something else as well: to become a separate person, everyone has to separate from those they love, and there is inevitably anger in that separation. From Kristeva’s point of view, anger at someone you love is not proof that there is no love, but part of the living bond between two different people. What matters is that it finds its outlet in words, not in something that could wound.
anger_at_loved.practice: Finish the sentence: “I’m angry with you because I need…” What comes after “need” is often exactly what you can later say calmly.

ambivalence.text: To love and be unable to stand the same person at the same time is agonizing, but deeply human. In Tales of Love, Kristeva examines Romeo and Juliet and shows that even in the most famous love story, hatred stands beside desire — and this is no accident but part of the experience of love. And in her book on Melanie Klein she explains that the psyche matures when it stops dividing loved ones into “all good” and “all bad” and learns to hold both images in one person. Klein called this the “depressive position” — not an illness but a stage of maturity. From this point of view, your mixed feelings are not a malfunction but a sign that you see the person whole.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a sheet of paper into two columns: “What I love about them” and “What I can’t stand about them.” Notice that both columns are true.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after someone leaves, after a breakup, or even after the death of a seriously ill loved one can be frightening: “How can I feel this?” But relief and love get along perfectly well together. In her book on Melanie Klein, Kristeva shows that love and heaviness, tenderness and weariness are always intertwined in close relationships. When long tension finally lets go, the psyche exhales — and that is not betrayal but the reaction of a living person who has carried a great deal. From Kristeva’s perspective, the shame here comes from wanting our feelings to be “pure,” all one color. But the psyche is never uniform. Relief does not cancel your love and grief — it speaks of how long you held on.
guilty_relief.practice: Tell yourself: “I feel relief, and I love.” Notice that both halves of the sentence can be true at once.

indifference.text: Indifference where something “ought” to move you — an event, a tragedy, someone’s joy — is frightening: what if I have no feelings? But this state doesn’t mean you are a bad person. In Black Sun, Kristeva describes how a psyche overloaded by pain or loss can muffle the link between words and feelings: a person understands what is happening but doesn’t feel it. She treated this with respect — as a defense, not a vice. From Kristeva’s perspective, indifference often means not an absence of feelings but their freezing: there’s too much, and the psyche is protecting itself. Feelings come back not on command but gradually, through small, bodily, unhurried impressions.
indifference.practice: Don’t force yourself to feel. Just note: “It’s quiet in me right now.” And ask: “What came before this — maybe too much?”

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your familiar role — and go somewhere no one knows you can be very strong. It’s an understandable feeling. In Strangers to Ourselves, Kristeva describes the foreigner sympathetically, as someone who once left their origins and gained a particular freedom for it: they are no longer defined only by where they come from. From Kristeva’s perspective, the dream of escape is a wish to become a “subject in process” again, not frozen in a single role. But she honestly shows the cost as well: a new place doesn’t cancel our inner strangeness — we take it with us. So it’s worth asking which role you want to leave behind — and where change could be let in right now.
escape.practice: Finish the sentence: “If I ran away, I could finally…” Then think about what tiny part of that you could try here.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is “off limits” — an unavailable person, the “wrong” person — can be confusing and unsettling. Many people know this feeling, and in itself it decides nothing for you. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva shows that prohibition and desire are born together: a prohibition doesn’t just restrain desire, it outlines its object and lends it a special allure. And in Tales of Love she traces how culture, from the troubadours to Don Juan, has told again and again of love at the edge of the permitted. From Kristeva’s perspective, such attraction often speaks not only of the person but of what you are missing — freedom, recognition, aliveness.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself, without judging: “What does this attraction promise me, besides the person themselves?” Write down one word.

social_anxiety.text: Shyness and fear of other people’s eyes can make any social contact hard, and you are far from alone in this. In Strangers to Ourselves, Kristeva writes about the stranger — a person who feels out of place among others. Following Freud, she shows that everyone knows this feeling from the inside: in each of us there is something strange, awkward, something that doesn’t match the proper image. The people around you who seem so confident also carry this strangeness within them. From Kristeva’s point of view, shyness is not your personal defect but a sharp experience of a shared condition. If everyone is a little foreign, then being awkward among people is not the exception but the general rule — and you can forgive yourself for it.
social_anxiety.practice: At your next gathering, choose one person and silently remind yourself: “They feel awkward sometimes too.” Notice whether anything changes in your body.

quote.text: The foreigner is within me, hence we are all foreigners. If I am a foreigner, there are no foreigners.
quote.author: Julia Kristeva

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty — not knowing what will happen next — can be exhausting, and the wish for clarity is completely natural. Kristeva described the human being as a “subject in process” and liked to compare the psyche to an “open system” — like a living organism that exists only as long as it exchanges with the world and changes. A closed system looks stable, but it freezes. From Kristeva’s perspective, uncertainty is the price of openness: as long as you are alive and connected to others, the future cannot be fully known. That doesn’t make the anxiety pleasant. But it can shift your view: you don’t have to know how it will all end. It’s enough to stay open and take the next step.
uncertainty.practice: Write: “I don’t know what will happen with…”, and below it: “But I know that today I can…” Finish with one simple thing.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, for results, for news — can be agonizing: time drags, and there’s nothing you can do. This is a normal reaction. Kristeva uses the phrase “subject in process,” and in French it is ambiguous: en procès also means “on trial.” From Kristeva’s perspective, waiting feels so heavy because it resembles waiting for a verdict: as if the answer will decide who you are. But her idea is that the “I” is always in process, and no single decision will define it once and for all. The result may change a great deal in your circumstances, but not your worth. And while your body waits, you can give it its own rhythm — footsteps, breathing, a simple task.
waiting.practice: Keep your hands busy with something rhythmic for a few minutes — take a walk, wash a cup, fold some clothes — and notice how time feels.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn’t do can keep coming back, and that is a sign that you cared. Kristeva wrote a book on Hannah Arendt and especially valued her idea that a human life is a story that continues as long as we live. Arendt saw in forgiveness the capacity to release a person from the consequences of the past so they can begin anew. In Black Sun, Kristeva also speaks of forgiveness — not as forgetting, but as the gift of a new meaning to what happened. From this point of view, the past cannot be changed, but its place in your story can: instead of a final full stop, it can become a chapter after which something began.
regret.practice: Describe the situation you regret in one sentence, and in the next, what this story changed in you or taught you.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person — their voice, their presence, your conversations — can be almost physical, and there is nothing excessive about it. In Tales of Love, Kristeva shows that a loved one becomes part of our inner world: we talk with them in our minds, they live in our imagination, in the way we look at things. Absence doesn’t erase this; it makes the inner bond sharper. From Kristeva’s perspective, longing is love that lacks a meeting, and it needs at least a form. Kristeva always emphasized that signs — words, letters, memories — are born in the place of absence. To give longing words is to give the bond a place where it can live.
longing.practice: Write this person a short letter that you don’t have to send. Tell them one thing about today.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from grim news, wars, injustice — speaks of your capacity for compassion, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva notes that the horrifying both repels and attracts: we want to turn away — and can’t tear our eyes off it. From Kristeva’s perspective, you can see why an endless news feed is so draining: it holds us in this oscillation, letting us neither make sense of things nor grieve. Culture, for Kristeva, has always answered horror with form — ritual, art, words that let us live through it and name it. To carry the world’s pain without breaking, it too needs a form: meaningful, limited contact with the news, a conversation, a cause you take part in.
world_pain.practice: Choose one piece of news that moved you and give it a form: write down what you feel, or do one small thing connected to it.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts in the most literal sense, and how deeply it stings doesn’t make you weak. Kristeva named her central idea “abjection,” from the Latin abjectus — “cast off.” She shows that every person, in order to define themselves, casts off whatever doesn’t fit within their boundaries. From Kristeva’s perspective, rejection wounds so deeply because it awakens an ancient fear of being cast off oneself. But her analysis says something else too: pushing away is the work of someone else’s boundaries, someone else’s fears, someone else’s history. When you are rejected, it speaks of what the other person needed at that moment, not of what you are worth.
rejection.practice: Write: “I was rejected in…” — and name the specific situation, not yourself as a whole. Notice the difference.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can go very deep, as if the ground were giving way beneath you. There is an explanation for this feeling, and it doesn’t make you “too dependent.” Kristeva, following psychoanalysis, reminds us that a human being begins in total dependence on others: an infant survives only if it is held and not left alone. This experience doesn’t disappear; it remains in us as the earliest layer. From Kristeva’s perspective, the fear of abandonment is an echo of that first helplessness, sounding when present bonds feel fragile. But since then you have gathered what the infant didn’t have: words, memory, connections, the experience of having already lived through separations. The adult “I” can hold itself while the fear is sounding.
abandonment.practice: Place your palm on your chest and tell yourself: “I’m here now, and I won’t abandon myself.” Then think of one person who stays in touch with you.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is one of humanity’s oldest stories, and the pain of it is real. In Tales of Love, Kristeva considers love as a work of the imagination: we create an ideal and grow as we reach toward it. She examines the myth of Narcissus, the troubadours who sang of an unattainable Lady, the mystics — and shows that love, even when unanswered, changes the one who loves. From Kristeva’s perspective, unrequited love is not a pointless waste: in it you discovered in yourself a capacity for tenderness, admiration, an ideal. That capacity is yours; it doesn’t depend on the other’s answer. The pain is still pain. But what awoke in you does not vanish along with the hope of being loved back.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love awakened in you — which qualities, desires, dreams. That is what will remain yours.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: as if you had been stripped of your dignity in front of others. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva shows how people and groups shore up their shaky boundaries by casting someone into the position of the “low,” the “unclean,” the “not like us.” From Kristeva’s perspective, the one who humiliates is often protecting their own fragility: they need someone to be lower in order to feel whole themselves. This doesn’t excuse the one who humiliates, but it clarifies the main thing: the place they tried to put you in is a projection of someone else’s fear, not the truth about you. Your dignity is not created by another’s gaze, and it cannot be revoked by it.
humiliation.practice: Write: “They tried to put me in the position of…”, and below it one thing you know about your dignity, whatever happened.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be tormenting and draining, and a great many people know it. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva shows that ideas of a “clean” and “proper” body are created by culture: she examines the biblical purity laws and shows that above all they draw boundaries — what is permitted and what is not. From Kristeva’s perspective, body shame largely speaks the language of such cultural codes: today’s models of the “right” body are also a system of rules, not nature. But for Kristeva the body is also a source of the semiotic: voice, rhythm, breath, touch, from which our whole life grows. It exists not to be looked at but to be lived in.
body_shame.practice: Choose one sensation your body is giving you right now — warmth, breath, the support of your feet — and stay with it for half a minute, without judging how you look.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, it’s frightening and exhausting, and there is room here for fear, anger and grief alike. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva writes about the “clean and proper” body — the image of a whole, obedient body on which our “I” relies. Illness disrupts this image: the body suddenly turns out to be foreign, unpredictable, as if not quite mine. From Kristeva’s perspective, you can understand why illness wounds not only physically but also your sense of self. At the same time, Kristeva, who wrote a great deal about disability, insisted that vulnerability is not an exception to human life but its common foundation, and it connects people rather than separating them. Your worth does not depend on how well your body works.
illness.practice: Say one sentence to your body, as you would to someone close who is struggling: “I’m with you.” Notice what responds.

pride.text: Pride in what you’ve done is a good, well-earned feeling, and you don’t need to hide it out of modesty. In Tales of Love, Kristeva writes at length about narcissism and, unlike everyday usage, doesn’t consider it a vice. For her, healthy narcissism is the foundation of the psyche: without some love for yourself and your image, you can neither love others nor act. She shows that our “I” is built around an ideal — who we would like to be. From Kristeva’s perspective, pride is a moment when you and your ideal briefly meet: what you’ve done matches what you hold dear. Such meetings nourish you and give you strength for the next step. Let yourself feel them fully.
pride.practice: Write down exactly what you did and which of your values it expresses. Read it aloud, and don’t play it down.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness, melancholy, is a state with much depth and beauty in it, and there’s no need to hurry it. The title of Kristeva’s book Black Sun comes from a sonnet by Gérard de Nerval: that is what the poet called melancholy. Kristeva explores it as an ancient experience of losing something that cannot be named. But the book’s central question is how people turn this sorrow into forms: into paintings, novels, music. For Kristeva, beauty is one such form: it seems to give loss a dignified face and lets it live in us without destroying us. From this point of view, your gentle sadness is a relative of art: in it, loss has already found a melody. You can stay in it for a while and listen to what it sings.
melancholy.practice: Find a piece of music, a painting or a poem in tune with your mood, and spend a few minutes with it.

quote.text: My only star is dead, — and my constellated lute bears the black sun of Melancholia.
quote.author: Gérard de Nerval
quote.source: the sonnet “El Desdichado” (1854); this line gave Kristeva’s book Black Sun its title
